u01s1l1: Hevalo, the deer who is your guide, leads you to a blue gate, where a man with a black moustache gives you a red apple. You take a bite, and Hevalo eats the rest.
u01s1l2: “Ez Hamo me,” says the man, and offers apple after apple, then teaches you how to refuse: “Na, spas.” When one drops on his head, Hamo rubs it: “Ez baş im!”
u01s1l3: At the gate you have your first talk: Hamo asks how you are, and you ask him back. Then he asks Hevalo, who has an apple in each cheek and only crunches.
u01s1l4: Hamo goes over it all with you: hello, how are you, yes please, no thanks. Hevalo nods at any question with an apple in it and looks at the sky for the rest.
u01s2l1: Under the oldest apple tree Hamo brings a tray: tea, warm bread, spring water and milk for Hevalo. You eat the bread, and Hevalo drinks his milk, loudly.
u01s2l2: Hamo turns the tray into a game, “Ev çi ye?”, and you name the tea, the bread, the water. Everything is xweş, says Hamo, and Hevalo agrees by eating the napkin.
u01s2l3: Hamo runs back to the blue gate to welcome you properly, with a bow: “Bi xêr hatî!” Then the tea comes, very hot, and Hevalo helpfully blows on the bread.
u01s2l4: Glass after glass, Hamo pours and you name what is on the tray, and his moustache lifts at every right answer. By the fifth glass, Hevalo has eaten the bread.
u01s3l1: Hamo asks your name at last and writes it in the dust with a stick, so as not to forget it. Hevalo rubs it out with a hoof, then looks at the sky, all innocence.
u01s3l2: Hamo shows you round: the blue gate creaks and the kitchen door sticks. Hevalo, hungry as ever, waits by the one small door that stays shut, the apple store.
u01s3l3: You ask Hamo the Kurdish for everything, and he knows it all until you point at an old tool over the stove: “Ez nizanim!” Then Hevalo knocks over your tea.
u01s3l4: Hamo plays guess-who with you round the house and its photos. Hevalo pretends to be a chair to escape, so Hamo sits on him, and the game ends in laughter.
u01s4l1: At supper you ask for bread: “Ez nan dixwazim.” Hamo never needs to ask Hevalo, who only wants apples, and for you he has two words: “Bixwe, vexwe!”
u01s4l2: The apple basket is empty, and a certain deer is lying very still under the table. But the water is cold, the tea is hot, and Hamo, who has a whole orchard, laughs.
u01s4l3: Hamo says “Şev baş!” at the guest-room door, and the next morning he is at the gate with tea: “Roj baş!” Ten steps down the lane, Hevalo turns back for an apple.
u01s4l4: On a morning walk with Hevalo you say hello and goodbye to half the village. At the blue gate Hamo has tea and news: the neighbours are coming tomorrow.
u02s1l1: While the tea brews, Hamo shows you the photo wall: his father, with a grand moustache and a flute, and his mother, with laughing eyes, both far away in Kobanî.
u02s1l2: The next photo shows all four children in a row: Hamo, his brother and his two sisters. “Em malbat in,” he says proudly, and straightens every frame, twice.
u02s1l3: The neighbours knock at the blue gate: Nazê with warm bread, Baran, and little Hêvî behind her. You are a guest, says Hamo, and Hevalo just eats the orchard.
u02s1l4: Hamo shows the neighbours the photos of his family. Then Baran finds the funniest one, Hamo at ten with no moustache, and Hamo turns it to the wall, too late.
u02s2l1: Nazê introduces her son Baran and her daughter Hêvî. Then Hêvî and Hamo count the hens in the yard, but the hens will not stand still: yek, du, yek, du.
u02s2l2: Dapîr Şemsê counts three hens, Hêvî four, and Hamo five, because he counted Hevalo. Baran’s grandfather, in the next village, has a donkey even older than Bozo.
u02s2l3: Round the tea tray Hêvî holds up six fingers, and Hevalo, says Hamo, is five, or eats like five deer. Dapîr counts her grandchildren and runs out of fingers.
u02s2l4: Dapîr and Hêvî count the hens again and finally agree, just as one walks out of the gate. Hamo counts his apples, nine, not ten, and Hevalo looks at the sky.
u02s3l1: The neighbours come back for breakfast on a cloth on the floor. Hamo boils eggs, seven for seven people, and an eighth for Hevalo, who never eats them.
u02s3l2: Baran says he is nine, nearly ten, so not a child, and drinks his milk to prove it. It leaves him a white moustache, which Hamo inspects like an expert.
u02s3l3: Nazê made the bread, and Hamo teaches you what to say to her: “Destê te sax be!” You are thirsty, and every time you say thank you, he fills your glass again.
u02s3l4: The breakfast cloth is spread in the yard for everyone. You thank Nazê properly, and Hamo says “Noşî can be!” to every single mouthful, Hevalo’s included.
u02s4l1: Everyone says which animals they have: Nazê a cat, Dapîr hens and a goat, Hamo a dog, Şêro, and a donkey, Bozo, who puts his big grey head over the wall.
u02s4l2: Hêvî is little, says Baran, but she has Hevalo, whose very name means “friend”. Meanwhile Hamo stirs five sugars into his tea and calls it a little sweetness.
u02s4l3: At supper Hamo passes round the bread: “Kerem bike!” Hêvî counts to ten without a mistake, and while you tell Dapîr where you are from, Hevalo eats your bread.
u02s4l4: A game at supper: everyone says one thing they have and one they don’t. Hevalo has no apples, so everyone gives him one: now he has six, and Hamo none.
u03s1l1: Hamo gives you a grand house tour, as if you were a visiting governor: a room, a window, a table. Hevalo checks every chair for an apple, and finds one.
u03s1l2: In every room something is in the wrong place: a hen on the bedding, a shoe on the table. Hamo carries the hen back to the yard, and she gives him an offended look.
u03s1l3: Up on the flat roof, where everyone sleeps in summer, Hamo sits you down with tea and tenûr bread. Then Baran shouts: he has found an old map with an X!
u03s1l4: Map in hand, Hamo checks that the X is not in the house: not in a room, not on the roof, not in the tenûr. Then he swears he has never seen this map before.
u03s2l1: The map starts in Hamo’s own orchard. Red is the best colour in the world, Hamo declares, because of the apples, and Hevalo votes for red by eating one.
u03s2l2: The next clue is a yellow flower by an old door, and Sêvan has a hundred of each. Hamo shows you his new green door; Hevalo eats a yellow flower, to be sure.
u03s2l3: “Binêre!” Hamo points at Dapîr’s white goat: her long beard and his moustache are the finest in the village. The next clue hangs on her collar, and she is eating it.
u03s2l4: The clues lead past the red apples to the white goat and the walnut tree. Then a fresh yellow X turns up on the window, and Hêvî giggles, with yellow on her fingers.
u03s3l1: The goat’s clue says: under the walnut tree. But Hamo cannot find his cap, until Hêvî pats her own head, “Ser!”, and points: it has been on his all morning.
u03s3l2: In Hêvî’s game Hamo calls out eyes, ears, head, and everyone touches them, Hevalo with his nose. You wash your hands for lunch, and a clue turns up in the tenûr.
u03s3l3: Behind the walnut tree Hevalo’s nose finds a rusty tin, with marbles and half an old photo: little Hamo and his sister. The other half, says Hamo softly, is in Kobanî.
u03s3l4: Hamo tells the story of the tin: summers with his aunt, when he and his sister buried it under this walnut tree and never dug it up. Hevalo sniffs every marble.
u03s4l1: Hamo shows you the school, where Xezo from Amed teaches; the shop, never open when you need it; and the spring, so cold that Hevalo drinks with his eyes shut.
u03s4l2: From the roof you see the mountain, the town below, the sheep and Ferhad’s cow. The sun goes down behind the mountain, just to show off, says Hamo.
u03s4l3: On the roof in the evening, as the birds sing in the apple trees, Hamo has news: tomorrow is market day in town! Hevalo cannot keep still: the town has new apples.
u03s4l4: At sunset you and Hamo name the village from the roof: the school, the shop, the spring, the mountain. Tomorrow you all go to town, Bozo too, if he agrees.
u04s1l1: Market day, and you are coming too. Bozo carries the empty baskets and stops at every flower to admire the view, says Hamo, who stops at every neighbour.
u04s1l2: On the way Hamo names all he sees: the river, the mountain, a hen from the village. At the river he looks at his moustache in the water, and finds it beautiful.
u04s1l3: Hamo knows every seller, and Mîrza best of all. Mîrza asks if you speak Kurdish, and you do, while Hevalo stands very still by the apples: only looking, for now.
u04s1l4: Hamo shows you round the market: Mîrza is selling, the baker is shouting, and Bozo is eating the seller’s blue flowers. You see more than he does, says Hamo.
u04s2l1: At the stall Hamo asks for tomatoes and potatoes, and the seller asks what he wants to eat this week. Fruit, says Hamo, eyeing the apples; Hevalo eyes them too.
u04s2l2: Hamo says he can carry everything and can tell a fresh fish by its eyes. He gives the bags to Bozo, and when a fish looks back at him, he decides on meat.
u04s2l3: Hamo takes three spoonfuls of sugar in Mîrza’s tea, then a fourth: “Zêde!” cries Mîrza. Hamo asks how you take yours, then adds two spoonfuls to it himself.
u04s2l4: Lunch in the market: bread, cheese and tea. Everyone eats, Hamo most of all, except Hevalo, who is not hungry and gazes at the mountain, not the apple.
u04s3l1: Hamo reads the prices aloud, shocked by each: twenty for grapes, thirty for a basket! “Hemû bi çend e?” he asks a seller, then counts his money three times.
u04s3l2: Hamo and Mîrza haggle over a basket of apples for ten minutes. In the end Hamo pays fifty and says it was cheap; “Bes e!” says Mîrza, and they both laugh.
u04s3l3: Hamo adds up his shopping and gets a thousand; you get a hundred and ten. So Hamo pays a hundred and ten, and a little more for the tea and the sugar.
u04s3l4: Hamo adds it all up again and has twenty left, exactly the price of a glass of tea, so he spends it on tea. Then Mîrza looks at his apple basket and goes pale.
u04s4l1: Mîrza’s apple basket is empty, and nobody knows who ate the apples. Bozo looks away, and Hevalo shakes his head so fast that Hamo says it for him: “Ez nizanim!”
u04s4l2: Hamo turns detective: is it true that Hevalo was by the basket? Hevalo says that is wrong, but his belly is very full and there is apple peel on his nose.
u04s4l3: At the apple trial Hevalo has apple all over his face, so nobody believes Hamo and everyone laughs. Then Lorîn phones from Kobanî: come for the weekend!
u04s4l4: Home at sunset, Bozo groaning under the bags. At the blue gate Hamo stops: Lorîn says come to Kobanî, all of you, and of course you want to go too.
u05s1l1: Dapîr’s calendar hangs by the stove, and Hamo explains the week: it starts on Saturday, the day of the trip. Sunday is a holiday, he says, and so is every day.
u05s1l2: Baran reads on Monday and reads more on Tuesday. Hamo nods wisely: in his day they read under the walnut tree, so now he can only read in the shade.
u05s1l3: Hamo bakes bread on Wednesday, writes to his mother on Thursday, then asks how long you will stay in Sêvan. As long as there are apples, says Hevalo’s face.
u05s1l4: Everyone writes their week on Dapîr’s calendar: “çay” every day for Hamo, “sêv” every day for Hevalo. Then Dapîr circles Saturday in red, twice.
u05s2l1: Hamo names the months like old friends: Adar brings Newroz, and Nîsan the blossom on the apple trees. And Friday, he says, is for tea and doing nothing.
u05s2l2: Hêvî wants the first present, and Hamo doesn’t know his own birthday. The day of the big snow, says Dapîr; the first snow, says Hamo; the second, says Dapîr.
u05s2l3: Nobody knows Hamo’s birthday, so he has one today, and again tomorrow. He can’t remember his age, but don’t worry, he says: his moustache is still young.
u05s2l4: Hamo and the children count the days to Saturday and the months to Newroz. Baran asks why there is no month for apples, and Hevalo agrees.
u05s3l1: Hamo has three clocks, each telling a different time: eleven, twelve, a quarter past something. He trusts the one that says it is time for tea, morning and evening.
u05s3l2: Hamo wakes with the rooster, gets up when the tea is ready and washes at the spring; after lunch he sleeps for “just five minutes”, which last an hour.
u05s3l3: Lunch is at noon, and Hamo arrives at one o’clock, delighted; Nazê laughs over the wall. Hamo is never late, he says: everyone else is just early.
u05s3l4: Hamo’s day runs from tea at seven to tea at nine at night, with a short nap that is not short. Then he sets his alarm for the bus: eight o’clock, but which eight?
u05s4l1: Hamo admits that he is sometimes late, and Nazê coughs; often late, and Dapîr coughs. Then he goes to the orchard to tell the apple trees about his work.
u05s4l2: Baran explains the bus: it leaves the square at eight and waits for nobody. “Belê, belê,” says Hamo, already planning a glass of tea at five to eight.
u05s4l3: The bus leaves at eight sharp on Saturday, with no time for tea. Hamo gives his solemn word, “Soza min soz e!”: if the bus will not stop, he will run after it.
u05s4l4: Hamo’s alarm is set for eight in the evening, not the morning. Hevalo races after the bus, but it leaves for Kobanî without them, and Hamo phones Lorîn.
u06s1l1: Ferhad’s tractor takes everyone to the main road, where a minibus driver squeezes you all in, Hevalo too. The driver is fast: “Hêdî, hêdî!” says Hamo.
u06s1l2: Kobanî has grown since Hamo was a boy: he turns left every time a sign says right, and gets lost looking for Lorîn’s street. “Here rasterast!” he tells himself.
u06s1l3: Kobanî at last, with Miştenûr hill high above the roofs. Lorîn calls down from upstairs, and Hamo calls back up, stopping on every stair to admire the view.
u06s1l4: Hevalo trots straight down the street to the family house, where Hamo’s mother opens the door. Lorîn comes downstairs: she knows why her brother is here.
u06s2l1: “Werin hundir! Rûnin!” calls Edûl, Hamo’s mother, and Lorîn’s children climb all over their uncle. Then she sends him to wash his hands, as if he were a boy.
u06s2l2: At Edûl’s table the orders never stop: “Bixwe! Vexwe! Bide min!” Hamo’s uncle and aunt bring more food, and he eats everything, and is given it all again.
u06s2l3: Hamo wants four sugars, and his mother says “Neke!”; he wants to go out alone, and she says “Neçe!” Then he whispers: is the other half of the photo with Lorîn?
u06s2l4: After dinner Lorîn brings out the other half of the photo, kept for years in an old book. Hamo’s father, Ibrahîm, looks at it and takes down his old flute.
u06s3l1: Hamo lists what he must do in Kobanî: climb Miştenûr, buy his father a book, visit his aunt, take Hevalo along. Then he adds “drink tea” to every line.
u06s3l2: In Edûl’s house women and men both help, and every man suddenly needs a rest. Hamo asks to take you up Miştenûr: after the washing-up, says his mother.
u06s3l3: The bookseller is closing, but he opens the door for Ibrahîm’s boy, and laughs at Hamo’s order, a book of proverbs for his father: they came from Ibrahîm.
u06s3l4: Hamo gives his father the book of proverbs, and Ibrahîm laughs: half of them are his. It is late, says Edûl; one more, says Ibrahîm, and reads ten.
u06s4l1: The old baker remembers Hamo as the boy who ate the crusts on the way home. The children argue about train, plane or taxi, and Hevalo votes for on foot.
u06s4l2: Packing: a heap of shoes, bags and parcels. Hamo sorts it all out: this bag is his, that one is yours, and nothing belongs to Hevalo except the apples.
u06s4l3: On the last evening Ibrahîm promises to come for Newroz, but snow is coming and the road may close, so Hamo sets three alarms and asks you to check them.
u06s4l4: At dawn Hamo is on time, for once. Edûl fills every bag with bread and cheese, the children shout goodbye, and the minibus climbs into the snow.
u07s1l1: The minibus climbs the pass in the first snow, and Hamo explains the weather to the driver: rain, snow, wind, sunshine. The driver already knew.
u07s1l2: Snowed in, Hamo tells the children about the seasons: winter is for soup and spring for roses. Hevalo fogs up the window, waiting for the warmth.
u07s1l3: A storm rattles the shutters as Hamo asks about the weather where you come from. Outside, Hevalo builds a snow-deer with an apple nose, then eats the nose.
u07s1l4: The sun is back, the snow melts and the stream by the walnut tree sings. Then Hamo’s mother phones from Kobanî: his father is ready, and she is coming too.
u07s2l1: Newroz is coming, and Hamo hands out the jobs: Baran will gather firewood, Nazê will sew clothes and Dapîr will bake. Hamo will light the fire, and supervise.
u07s2l2: The children count the days to Newroz, and Hamo’s great speech has gone missing. Bring it here, Hamo tells Hevalo, who is chewing something papery.
u07s2l3: Newroz is the spring festival and the new year, says Hamo, and he tells you of Kawa the blacksmith and his fires. Only his father knows the rest: two hours of it.
u07s2l4: Hamo practises his Newroz speech on the hens, who leave, and on Bozo, who leaves too. You stay to the end, so he gives it to you again, from the beginning.
u07s3l1: At the school Xezo teaches the children the govend, and Hamo tells you all about the drum and the zurna. Soon he joins the line, and so do the hens.
u07s3l2: Nazê has sewn new clothes, and Hamo puts on his suit with the green sash at once, over his pyjamas. He will lead the govend, he says, if his knees agree.
u07s3l3: The night before Newroz, Hamo shows you a full moon and a thousand stars. Then two lights come up the road from Kobanî: Hamo’s parents are here.
u07s3l4: Hamo’s parents are at the table and the firewood is on the hill. Tomorrow Baran will play the drum, his uncle the zurna, and Hamo will lead the govend.
u07s4l1: The whole village picnics on the hill for Newroz. At dusk Hamo lights the fire, and everyone jumps over it for good health, Hamo holding his moustache.
u07s4l2: By the dying fire Hamo’s father plays his old flute, then gives it to Hamo: keep the song going. Hamo’s first squeak sends Hevalo bolting, and everyone laughs.
u07s4l3: The morning after the govend, Hamo cannot get out of bed: “Pişta min diêşe!” His back is very bad, he says, and he asks for tea, honey and sympathy, in that order.
u07s4l4: From his bed Hamo tells everyone about Newroz: the fire, the flute, the speech nobody heard. When his mother phones, he says his back is a little better.
u08s1l1: Hamo lies in bed and lists everything that hurts, from his legs to his shoulders. Rest, says Nazê, but Hamo has been resting since breakfast, and it is exhausting.
u08s1l2: Hamo has a sore neck, a cough and probably a fever, and he is very sad until he hears the doctor is coming. Then he hides the honey and looks almost cheerful.
u08s1l3: At the word “hospital” Hamo is much better, and he tells you about his tooth while Doctor Azad listens to his chest. Healthy, says the doctor: he just talks a lot.
u08s1l4: From his bed Hamo plans next Newroz, and every neighbour hears a longer list of what hurts. All that is wrong with him, says Doctor Azad, is his patience.
u08s2l1: Doctor Azad listens to Hamo’s heart and presses his back. Pills, please, not the needle, says Hamo; the doctor laughs: he will be better in a week.
u08s2l2: Walk every day, says the doctor, and no honey at night. Then each neighbour brings honey, and the doctor gives every jar to you to guard: he knows Hamo.
u08s2l3: In the morning a honey jar is empty and Hamo’s moustache is sticky. Hamo swears he is innocent; Hevalo, who for once is innocent, looks offended.
u08s2l4: The honey case is closed: Doctor Azad finds a sticky spoon under Hamo’s pillow, and takes the last jar home, for safety. Hamo is better, but sad.
u08s3l1: Back on his feet, Hamo compares everyone: who is taller, who is older, who is cleverer. He is the cleverest of all, he says, and his moustache the longest.
u08s3l2: Hamo asks everyone their favourite season, fruit and place; Hevalo’s answer is always the same. Hamo’s is Sêvan, whose apples are famous as far as Kobanî.
u08s3l3: At the tea house contest Ferhad’s moustache is longer, but everyone agrees Hamo’s is the most beautiful. Hamo promises Ferhad the prize next year.
u08s3l4: Hamo walks with you and Hevalo every day, stopping to talk to everyone. The best medicine, he says, is mountain air, and the second best is tea.
u08s4l1: Baran comes home late one evening, muddy to the knees, and says nothing. Hêvî is amazed that her brother is so quiet; Hamo has a feeling, and will wait.
u08s4l2: Baran sits alone on the flat roof. Hamo climbs up and sits beside him without a word, then talks quietly about trust, and the truth being better than a lie.
u08s4l3: At eight, Hamo tells you, he lost his father’s best ram and hid all day, afraid to go home. That evening he told his father everything, and his father called him brave.
u08s4l4: Baran comes down from the roof and sits by the stove, but he will not tell yet: “Sibe ez ê bibêjim.” Then Hevalo offers him his last apple: a very big moment.
u09s1l1: At breakfast Baran takes a deep breath, and the whole table goes quiet: “Duh ez çûm çem.” He was by the river with Bozo, when suddenly something happened.
u09s1l2: Baran goes on: Bozo saw a goat across the valley and ran, and Baran ran after him over the stones and along the cliffs. He never caught him, and was left all alone.
u09s1l3: Baran was a little afraid, he admits: he sat down under a walnut tree to think, and fell asleep. Hamo says that he himself would have eaten some walnuts first.
u09s1l4: Baran followed the stars home, not afraid at all, he says, and found Bozo eating Dapîr’s mint. But on the way he saw smoke from a tent where nobody lives.
u09s2l1: Hamo strokes his moustache and remembers: as a boy he spent every summer in Sêvan, all day in the orchard. The summers were longer then, says Dapîr.
u09s2l2: At nine, one dark night, Hamo met a wolf as big as a horse, or was it a bear? He phones his mother in Kobanî, and she laughs: it was the neighbours’ dog.
u09s2l3: A boy on a mule brings a message from Bişar the shepherd: every night something wild and shy, like a deer, comes to his tent. Hevalo’s ears shoot up.
u09s2l4: Hamo tells his wolf story again, and the children tell it back with other animals, Hêvî with a clever fox. The best story is Dapîr’s, of a lamb in the snow.
u09s3l1: Hamo shows Baran how to tell a story in order, with the day he bought Bozo, which lasted from July to August. A good story, he says, is like tea: it needs time.
u09s3l2: Hamo retells Baran’s day as a hero’s journey: Baran walked, wandered and laughed at his fear. A bird flew over him, an eagle, says Hamo; a crow, says Dapîr.
u09s3l3: Hamo decides that this summer everyone goes up to Bişar’s tent on the zozan. The packing begins at once, and Bozo, hearing the word “zozan”, runs away again.
u09s3l4: Packing for the zozan: tents, ropes and four baskets of apples, for Bişar, says Hamo, while Hevalo says nothing. Only Bozo is cross: he does not want to go.
u09s4l1: Dapîr packs her saddlebags and tells you about her youth: her family had a horse, and she rode it up to the pastures and came down the mountain singing.
u09s4l2: The last time they moved, Hamo was a whole day late, by mistake. Tomorrow at dawn he will be wide awake, he says, and Bozo watches shyly from behind the wall.
u09s4l3: Hevalo follows Bozo’s tracks to the spring, and there is Bozo with Ferhad’s little donkey, refusing to come home. “Bozo evîndar e!” says Hamo, delighted.
u09s4l4: On the climb Dapîr shows you the rock where they rested and the spring where she filled her jug. Then a flock of sheep fills the path, and everyone laughs.
u10s1l1: The shepherd on the path is Bişar, Hamo’s old friend. Over tea on the rocks he asks what you saw, what you ate and what Bozo did, and Hamo tells it all, twice.
u10s1l2: Bişar asks what everyone saw on the climb: Baran an eagle, Hêvî flowers, Hamo nothing, as he was talking. And over the sheep, nobody heard a word Hamo said.
u10s1l3: At dusk a doe comes for Bişar’s salt and looks straight at Hevalo, who drops his apple. “Bêdeng!” whispers Hamo, and he leaves a sack of apples by the tent.
u10s1l4: By the fire Bişar says the doe comes every night for the salt, and Hamo names her Zerê, “the golden one”. By morning Hevalo is gone, and so is the sack of apples.
u10s2l1: Dawn on the zozan: Bişar teaches you to milk a ewe, and Hamo proudly spills half his milk. Dapîr rocks the goatskin churn until only the ayran is left.
u10s2l2: Dapîr and Nazê bake bread on the saj, each one thin as paper, and Hamo “helps” and burns one. Then you catch Hevalo slipping off with an apple: “Min tu dîtî!”
u10s2l3: The tracks of two deer lead to a hidden lake, where Hevalo and Zerê share apples, and to a ruined stone house. Who was its owner? Hamo asks you to guess.
u10s2l4: Back at the tents everyone tells what they saw at the lake. There is no zurna, but everyone sings and dances the govend, and Hevalo falls asleep dreaming of Zerê.
u10s3l1: At the old stone house Dapîr stops: it was her family’s summer home. She used to swim in the lake, make dried curd on that very roof and look after the lambs.
u10s3l2: One summer, when Dapîr was a girl, a young flute player from Kobanî played by the lake every evening: Hamo’s father. For once, Hamo has nothing to say.
u10s3l3: The last day on the zozan. Zerê gives Hevalo an apple and is gone into the grass. Everyone packs with a heavy heart, and Bişar promises to meet next summer.
u10s3l4: On the last evening Dapîr hums the flute player’s tune by the fire. Hamo writes the day in his notebook, his way: Hevalo took the sack, Bişar burned the bread.
u10s4l1: Back in Sêvan, Hamo shows the neighbours his photos of the summer, mostly of his thumb. The biggest event was Hevalo’s love: say “Zerê”, and his ears go up.
u10s4l2: Who said the doe was “just a goat”? Baran says Hamo did, and Hamo is astonished. A summer like no other, he says, to change the subject, and everyone agrees.
u10s4l3: Hamo writes the summer down in his old notebook. He is a little worried, as the apples are nearly ripe, but his hope is big: a good harvest, with you to help.
u10s4l4: Hamo reads the summer aloud from his notebook, and everyone corrects him: it was Hamo, not Bişar, who burned the bread. So Hamo writes it again, his way.
u11s1l1: September, and the apples are nearly ripe. Hamo shows you the village trades: the farmer, the worker, the cook, the builder. Each says his own is the best.
u11s1l2: The children play “what will you be?”: Baran a writer, Hêvî a nurse for the hens. Ferhad brings saplings, and Hamo says he will plant them, looking at you.
u11s1l3: News in the village: a big school in Hewlêr has offered Xezo a post. A great chance, Hamo says over tea, but Hewlêr is far. He asks what you would do.
u11s1l4: Hamo works in the orchard all day, and Ferhad, Mîrza and Bişar stop by, each sure his own work is the best. Hamo agrees with them all, and all go home happy.
u11s2l1: The harvest begins, and Hamo has a plan: ladders on the left, baskets on the right, tea in the middle. Dapîr, the most experienced, says nothing and keeps picking.
u11s2l2: Everyone picks, Hamo singing at the top of a ladder, until Bozo’s load is so heavy that he sits down. Then a cloud comes over the mountain, and everyone hurries.
u11s2l3: After the harvest the village meets. Ferhad wants every house to plant saplings, and Xezo says she will go to Hewlêr in the spring, and come back every Newroz.
u11s2l4: Xezo writes to the school in Hewlêr: yes, she will come in the spring. Mîrza takes the letter to the post, so the whole village knows by lunchtime.
u11s3l1: Xezo has set Baran’s class a task: a talk about Sêvan in front of the whole school. Baran is shy and his voice shakes. That is why, says Hamo, they will practise.
u11s3l2: Baran lists his fears: the hall is big, the children will laugh, his voice will shake. Hamo’s advice: speak loudly and slowly, like him. That, says Baran, is what he fears.
u11s3l3: Hamo helps Baran write his talk, letter by letter. Baran practises in front of the hens, and Hevalo, the most patient listener in the world, stamps a hoof in applause.
u11s3l4: Baran gives his talk in the school hall: Sêvan, its apples, its people, and Hevalo. Xezo says it was the best talk of the year, and Baran gives it again at home, twice.
u11s4l1: Hamo asks everyone their goals: Hêvî wants a cat, Nazê wants Hamo on time for once, and Hamo wants a new tea glass. Learning, he tells you, is one step at a time.
u11s4l2: Hamo remembers leaving Kobanî: go, said his father, but don’t forget your roots. When he first came here he was homesick, and the village gave him warmth.
u11s4l3: The first snow. Hamo lights the stove and plans a winter evening of tales every night, one of his father’s each time. He asks which you like better, a tale or a song.
u11s4l4: The last winter before Xezo leaves, and snow on every roof. Hamo, your storyteller, puts the tea on the stove and begins the first tale of the winter.
u12s1l1: Hamo begins the first tale: a mother goat tells her two kids, Şengê and Pengê, never to open the door. But the wolf is a liar, and makes his voice as soft as wool.
u12s1l2: The wolf knocks and sings like the kids’ mother. Hamo asks what will happen if they open the door, but clever Şengê sees the trick: under it are grey paws.
u12s1l3: The children turn the tale into a play by the stove. Hevalo gets the wolf and plays it terribly, far too friendly, pushing apples under the door with his hoof.
u12s1l4: Dapîr takes her spoon out of her tea: every tale, she says, is a piece of advice. Baran asks for another, and then, in the middle of a snowy night, someone knocks.
u12s2l1: A knock at midnight in deep snow: an old dengbêj and his grandson. Hamo spreads the meal cloth at once, and when they praise Sêvan, he pretends not to be pleased.
u12s2l2: Over dinner everyone talks at once, and Hamo passes it all on: the pass is closed until February, Baran complains, and who will tell Bişar his old friend is here?
u12s2l3: After dinner the old dengbêj sings kilams of the old days. His last is about a young flute player from Kobanî, Hamo’s father, but its last verse is lost.
u12s2l4: Hamo phones his father, who has left his phone at home again. When the snow stops the guests leave, and the whole village hums the unfinished song.
u12s3l1: The second night’s tale: the fox and the bear share a field, and the bear always gets the tasteless half. He sulks so loudly that Hevalo hides behind the stove.
u12s3l2: Dapîr answers every tale with a proverb, Hamo every proverb with a tale: drop by drop, water becomes a lake; a sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole.
u12s3l3: A proverb duel: you and the children against Dapîr, with Hamo as judge. Then Hevalo walks in with an apple in his mouth, his answer to every problem.
u12s3l4: Hamo’s phone rings: his father, from Kobanî. He sings the lost verse down the line, and Hamo, in tears, repeats it for everyone while Dapîr sings along.
u12s4l1: Spring, and Ferhad’s son’s wedding fills the square: the bride on a white horse, the big drum, the joyful cries. Hamo leads the govend, and even Bozo dances.
u12s4l2: Xezo makes her goodbye speech: thank you for every tale and every glass of tea. “Ez ê bêriya we hemûyan bikim,” she says, then turns to Hamo and cannot finish.
u12s4l3: Dawn at the blue gate, and the bus is waiting for Xezo. Hamo wishes her a safe journey, and she orders him to take care of his moustache. Hevalo gets the last apple.
u12s4l4: The bus has gone, and the village turns to you: your road is ending too. Everyone blesses you at the blue gate, and Hamo shows you the sapling he planted for you.
